sanskrit:
मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः।
आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत॥
transliteration:
mātrā-sparśās tu kaunteya śītoṣṇa-sukha-duḥkha-dāḥ
āgamāpāyino 'nityās tāṁs titikṣasva bhārata
translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These come and go; they do not last. Bear them patiently, O Arjuna.
meaning: Every feeling, good or bad, is a visitor, not a resident. If you remember that it will pass, you stop being thrown around by it.
explanation: Krishna begins with something everyone knows from daily life: the senses meet the world and we feel heat or cold, comfort or pain. His point is that these experiences are always moving. They arrive, stay a while and leave. The Sanskrit word titikṣā means patient endurance, a calm strength that lets you feel fully without being overturned. This is not about suppressing feelings. It is about knowing that you are bigger than any single feeling, so you can wait for it to pass and then act wisely.

keywords.meaning: contact of the senses with objects

story.title: Thirteen years in the forest
story.text: After losing everything in a game of dice, the Pandavas lived twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth in disguise. Heat, hunger and humiliation came and went. They endured, and when the years ended they were still themselves.

illustration.idea: Five brothers and Draupadi walking through a monsoon forest, calm faces under heavy rain.

teaching.title: Name the weather
teaching.practice: When a strong feeling arrives today, say to yourself: this is weather, and weather passes. Wait ten breaths before reacting.

test.question: According to this verse, pleasure and pain are...
What does Krishna ask Arjuna to do with them?

sanskrit:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः।
अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे॥
transliteration:
na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ
ajo nityaḥ śāśvato 'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre
translation: The Self is never born and never dies. It did not come into being and will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.
meaning: What you truly are is deeper than your body and your life story. That core cannot be harmed, which is a source of courage.
explanation: This is one of the most quoted verses of the Gita. Arjuna fears killing his elders, so Krishna lifts the conversation to a deeper level. The Self, called ātman, is not the body. It was not born when the body was born and does not end when the body ends. The verse piles up words for this: unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient. For a reader today, it offers a steady place inside that loss and failure cannot touch, which gives the courage to face hard things.

story.title: Nachiketa asks Death
story.text: In the Katha Upanishad, the boy Nachiketa is sent to Yama, the lord of death. Offered wealth and long life instead, he refuses and asks only one thing: what remains when a person dies? Yama, impressed, teaches him that the Self is never born and never dies.

illustration.idea: A young boy sitting fearlessly before a calm, regal Yama at the gate of a quiet palace.

teaching.title: Find the still centre
teaching.practice: Sit for two minutes and notice that thoughts and sensations change, but the one who notices them stays the same. Rest there.

test.question: What does this verse say about the Self?
options: It is never born and never dies

test.question: When the body is killed, the Self is...

sanskrit:
वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि।
तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णान्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही॥
transliteration:
vāsāṁsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya navāni gṛhṇāti naro 'parāṇi
tathā śarīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇāny anyāni saṁyāti navāni dehī
translation: Just as a person throws away worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied Self casts off worn-out bodies and enters new ones.
meaning: Change, even the biggest change, is like changing clothes. The wearer stays. This softens our fear of endings.
explanation: Krishna gives Arjuna a simple picture he can hold on to. We do not mourn an old shirt when we put on a new one. In the same way, the dehī, the one who lives in the body, moves from body to body. Indian tradition reads this as rebirth, but the verse also speaks to everyday change: jobs, homes and stages of life are outer clothing. Who you are underneath continues, and that makes letting go less frightening.

keywords.meaning: the one who dwells in the body

story.title: Arjuna lays down his bow
story.text: On the field of Kurukshetra, Arjuna sees his teachers, grandfather and cousins on the other side. Overcome with grief, he drops his bow and refuses to fight. Krishna begins his teaching by reminding him that bodies change, but the Self does not.

illustration.idea: Arjuna seated in his chariot with his bow on the floor, Krishna turning toward him with a gentle smile.

teaching.title: Let one old thing go
teaching.practice: Pick one old habit, belief or grudge that no longer fits you. Write it down, and decide to set it aside like a worn-out shirt.

test.question: What image does Krishna use in this verse?
Who 'changes clothes' in this teaching?

sanskrit:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि॥
transliteration:
karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana
mā karma-phala-hetur bhūr mā te saṅgo 'stv akarmaṇi
translation: You have a right to your actions alone, never to their results. Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, and do not be attached to doing nothing.
meaning: Put your whole heart into the work and let go of the outcome. Results depend on many things; your effort depends on you.
explanation: Perhaps the most famous line of the Gita. It has four parts: you have a right to act; you have no claim over the results; do not let results be your only motive; and do not use this as an excuse to do nothing. Krishna is not saying results do not matter. He is saying they are shaped by many forces beyond you, so tying your peace to them makes you anxious. Do your best, offer it, and let the outcome come. This is the seed of karma yoga, the path of selfless action.

story.title: The heart of Krishna's advice
story.text: Arjuna is frozen, afraid of what victory or defeat will cost. Krishna tells him that worrying about results is what paralyses him. His duty is to act well; the outcome is not his to own.

illustration.idea: Krishna pointing forward from the chariot at sunrise, Arjuna lifting his bow again.

teaching.title: Effort, not outcome
teaching.practice: Choose one task today and do it as well as you can without checking how it will be judged. Notice how much lighter it feels.

test.question: According to this verse, you have a right to...
Should you stop acting because results are uncertain?
options: No, do not be attached to inaction

sanskrit:
योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनञ्जय।
सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते॥
transliteration:
yoga-sthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṁ tyaktvā dhanañjaya
siddhy-asiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṁ yoga ucyate
translation: Established in yoga, perform your actions, giving up attachment, O Arjuna. Stay the same in success and failure. This evenness of mind is called yoga.
meaning: Yoga is not only a posture. It is a balanced mind that does not swing wildly between winning and losing.
explanation: Here the Gita gives one of its clearest definitions: yoga is samatvam, evenness. Krishna calls Arjuna Dhanañjaya, winner of wealth, a reminder of his past successes, and then asks him to hold success and failure with the same steady mind. This is not indifference. You still care and still try hard, but your balance does not depend on how things turn out. Many teachers see this verse as the bridge between action and meditation.

story.title: Yudhishthira's even mind
story.text: Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava, was known for staying steady whether he was crowned king or sent into exile. Even after great losses, he answered questions of dharma calmly, which is why he was called Dharmaraja.

illustration.idea: A calm king in simple forest clothes, seated beneath a banyan tree, half his face lit by sunset.

teaching.title: Same face for praise and blame
teaching.practice: The next time you get praise or criticism today, pause and respond with the same calm tone either way.

test.question: What does this verse call 'yoga'?
How should one be in success and failure?

sanskrit:
दुःखेष्वनुद्विग्नमनाः सुखेषु विगतस्पृहः।
वीतरागभयक्रोधः स्थितधीर्मुनिरुच्यते॥
transliteration:
duḥkheṣv anudvigna-manāḥ sukheṣu vigata-spṛhaḥ
vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodhaḥ sthita-dhīr munir ucyate
translation: One whose mind is not shaken by sorrow, who does not crave pleasure, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom.
meaning: Wisdom shows in how we handle hard times and good times. A steady mind is free of craving, fear and anger.
explanation: Arjuna asks what a truly wise person looks like, and Krishna paints the sthita-dhī, the one of steady mind. In sorrow they are not shaken; in pleasure they do not grasp for more. Three forces that usually drive us, attachment (rāga), fear (bhaya) and anger (krodha), have lost their hold. The word muni means a sage, often one who is quiet. The verse gives us a practical mirror: when these three rise in us, we know where our work lies.

story.title: Rama hears of his exile
story.text: In the Ramayana, on the morning Rama was to be crowned, he was told he must instead leave for the forest for fourteen years. The poet Valmiki says his face did not change. He accepted it with the same calm he would have shown on his coronation.

illustration.idea: Prince Rama bowing to his father in a palace hall, serene, while courtiers look on in shock.

teaching.title: Spot the three thieves
teaching.practice: Notice today when craving, fear or anger tries to take over a decision. Just naming which one it is weakens its grip.

test.question: A person of steady wisdom is free from...
In the story, how did Rama react to his exile?

sanskrit:
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते।
सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते॥
transliteration:
dhyāyato viṣayān puṁsaḥ saṅgas teṣūpajāyate
saṅgāt sañjāyate kāmaḥ kāmāt krodho 'bhijāyate
translation: When a person dwells on sense objects, attachment to them arises. From attachment comes desire, and from desire comes anger.
meaning: Trouble starts small, with what we keep thinking about. Watch your thoughts early and you stop the chain before it reaches anger.
explanation: This verse and the next describe a chain reaction in the mind. It begins innocently: we keep thinking about something we like. Thinking becomes attachment (saṅga). Attachment becomes desire (kāma). When desire is blocked, it turns into anger (krodha). The next verse continues: anger brings confusion, confusion destroys memory and judgement, and then a person falls. The teaching is hopeful, because the earliest link, where our attention goes, is the easiest place to step in.

story.title: Ravana's desire
story.text: In the Ramayana, Ravana hears of Sita's beauty and cannot stop thinking of her. That thought grows into obsession, then into the abduction of Sita, and finally into the war that destroys his kingdom.

illustration.idea: A brooding ten-headed king on a golden throne in Lanka, one hand clenched, dark clouds gathering behind.

teaching.title: Catch the first link
teaching.practice: When you notice yourself replaying something you want, gently switch your attention to something else before it turns into craving.

test.question: What does dwelling on sense objects lead to first?
According to this verse, anger comes from...

sanskrit:
तस्मादसक्तः सततं कार्यं कर्म समाचर।
असक्तो ह्याचरन्कर्म परमाप्नोति पूरुषः॥
transliteration:
tasmād asaktaḥ satataṁ kāryaṁ karma samācara
asakto hy ācaran karma param āpnoti pūruṣaḥ
translation: Therefore, always do the work that must be done, without attachment. By working without attachment, a person reaches the highest.
meaning: You do not need to run away from the world to grow spiritually. Doing your duties with a free heart is itself the path.
explanation: In chapter three Arjuna asks why he should act at all if knowledge is higher than action. Krishna answers that action is unavoidable, so the question is how to act. The key word is asakta, unattached. Do the work that is yours to do, kārya, steadily and without clinging to rewards. Such work purifies the mind and leads to the highest good. This makes spiritual life possible for ordinary people with jobs and families, not only for monks.

keywords.meaning: what ought to be done, duty

story.title: King Janaka
story.text: In the very next verse, Krishna names King Janaka as an example. Janaka ruled a kingdom, managed courts and armies, and yet was known as a sage, because he did his work without clinging to it.

illustration.idea: A king on a simple throne listening to petitioners, with a meditative stillness about him.

teaching.title: Do the next right thing
teaching.practice: Pick one duty you have been avoiding and do it today, simply because it needs doing.

test.question: How should necessary work be done?
Which king is given as an example of this teaching?

sanskrit:
यद्यदाचरति श्रेष्ठस्तत्तदेवेतरो जनः।
स यत्प्रमाणं कुरुते लोकस्तदनुवर्तते॥
transliteration:
yad yad ācarati śreṣṭhas tat tad evetaro janaḥ
sa yat pramāṇaṁ kurute lokas tad anuvartate
translation: Whatever a great person does, others follow. Whatever standard they set, the world follows it.
meaning: People learn more from what we do than from what we say. Anyone with influence, at home or at work, is setting an example.
explanation: Krishna explains why even a wise person who needs nothing should keep working: others are watching. The word śreṣṭha means the best or most respected person in a group. Whatever standard (pramāṇa) they set becomes the norm. Parents, teachers, managers and public figures all carry this responsibility. In the following verses Krishna says that he himself keeps acting, though he has nothing to gain, so that the world is not led astray.

story.title: Rama, the model king
story.text: In the Ramayana, Rama is remembered as maryada purushottama, the ideal person who keeps to right conduct. He kept his promises even when it cost him, and the people of Ayodhya modelled their lives on his example.

illustration.idea: Rama walking among ordinary townspeople in Ayodhya, children imitating his gentle posture.

teaching.title: Be the example
teaching.practice: Think of one person who looks up to you. Do one thing today that you would be happy for them to copy.

test.question: What do ordinary people do, according to this verse?
options: Follow the example of great people

test.question: What is the main lesson?
options: Leaders can do as they like
Our actions set standards for others

sanskrit:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात्।
स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः॥
transliteration:
śreyān sva-dharmo viguṇaḥ para-dharmāt sv-anuṣṭhitāt
sva-dharme nidhanaṁ śreyaḥ para-dharmo bhayāvahaḥ
translation: It is better to follow your own duty imperfectly than to follow another's duty perfectly. It is better even to die in your own duty; another's duty is full of danger.
meaning: Live your own life, not a copy of someone else's. Your own path, done imperfectly, is worth more than borrowed success.
explanation: Svadharma means your own dharma, the duty and path that fits your nature, abilities and situation. Paradharma is someone else's. Krishna says even an imperfect effort on your own path is better than a perfect copy of another's. Arjuna, a protector by role, wanted to escape into the life of a renunciate; Krishna warns that this would be living against his grain. Today it reminds us that comparison is costly and that authenticity is a form of courage.

story.title: The warrior who wanted to be a monk
story.text: Arjuna, a warrior by nature and duty, told Krishna he would rather live as a beggar than fight. Krishna reminds him that running from his own role into someone else's would not bring him peace.

illustration.idea: Arjuna imagining himself as a wandering monk in a thought bubble, while Krishna gently points to the bow beside him.

teaching.title: Stop comparing
teaching.practice: When you catch yourself envying someone's path today, ask: what is my own next step? Then take it.

test.question: Which is better, according to this verse?
options: Your own duty, even done imperfectly

test.question: What is 'svadharma'?

sanskrit:
यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत।
अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम्॥
transliteration:
yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata
abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham
translation: Whenever righteousness declines and unrighteousness rises, O Arjuna, then I manifest myself.
meaning: However dark things get, goodness is never abandoned. The divine steps in when the world needs it most.
explanation: In chapter four Krishna reveals that he has taken birth many times. This verse gives the reason. Dharma is the order that holds life together: truth, fairness, duty and care. When it weakens (glāni) and adharma rises, the divine takes form to restore balance. This verse, with the next, is the basis of the teaching of avatāras, divine descents. It also carries a promise of hope: no age is so dark that goodness is abandoned.

keywords.meaning: righteousness, the order that sustains life

story.title: The promise of the avatars
story.text: Indian tradition tells of Vishnu taking many forms, the avatars, to restore balance: Rama in the Treta age and Krishna in the Dvapara age among them. Here Krishna himself explains why he comes.

illustration.idea: A luminous blue figure appearing above a darkened world, light spreading outward like dawn.

teaching.title: Be part of the answer
teaching.practice: Notice one small wrong around you today, an unkind word or some litter, and quietly set it right.

test.question: When does Krishna say he manifests?
What is 'dharma' closest to in this verse?

sanskrit:
परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम्।
धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे॥
transliteration:
paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām
dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge
translation: To protect the good, to destroy evil, and to firmly establish righteousness, I come into being age after age.
meaning: Protecting the good and standing against harm is a sacred act. In every age, goodness is renewed.
explanation: This verse completes the previous one by naming the purpose of each divine descent: to protect the good (sādhu), to remove those who do harm, and to firmly re-establish dharma. The phrase yuge yuge, age after age, tells us this is not a single event but a recurring pattern. Many readers also take it inwardly: whenever our own inner goodness is threatened, a higher strength can rise within us to protect it.

story.title: Born in a prison
story.text: Krishna was born at midnight in the prison of the tyrant Kamsa, who feared him. The guards fell asleep, the doors opened, and his father Vasudeva carried the baby across the flooded Yamuna to safety in Gokul.

illustration.idea: A father wading through a stormy river at night, holding a baby in a basket above his head, a great serpent sheltering them.

teaching.title: Protect someone
teaching.practice: Stand up today for someone who is being treated unfairly, even in a small way.

test.question: Why does Krishna come 'age after age'?
options: To protect the good and establish righteousness

test.question: Where was Krishna born, according to tradition?

sanskrit:
विद्याविनयसम्पन्ने ब्राह्मणे गवि हस्तिनि।
शुनि चैव श्वपाके च पण्डिताः समदर्शिनः॥
transliteration:
vidyā-vinaya-sampanne brāhmaṇe gavi hastini
śuni caiva śva-pāke ca paṇḍitāḥ sama-darśinaḥ
translation: The wise see with an equal eye a learned and humble scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste.
meaning: True wisdom sees the same divine spark in every being, regardless of status, species or background.
explanation: This verse lists beings that society ranked very differently: a learned and humble scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste. The wise, paṇḍitāḥ, look at all of them with sama-darśana, an equal eye. This does not deny that people are different. It says the same divine reality is present in each, so dignity and respect are owed to all. It is one of the Gita's strongest statements against prejudice.

story.title: Shankara meets an outcaste
story.text: A traditional story tells that the philosopher Adi Shankara, walking in Kashi, asked an outcaste to move out of his way. The man asked whether he meant his body or his Self, since the Self is the same in all. Shankara bowed to him as his teacher.

illustration.idea: A young monk bowing before a humble man with four dogs on the ghats of a riverside city at dawn.

teaching.title: Equal eyes
teaching.practice: Greet everyone you meet today, the cleaner, the shopkeeper, the stranger, with the same warmth you would give an honoured guest.

test.question: How do the wise see all beings?
In the story, what did Shankara do after the conversation?
options: Bowed to the man as his teacher

sanskrit:
उद्धरेदात्मनात्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत्।
आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः॥
transliteration:
uddhared ātmanātmānaṁ nātmānam avasādayet
ātmaiva hy ātmano bandhur ātmaiva ripur ātmanaḥ
translation: Lift yourself up by your own self; do not let yourself sink down. For the self alone is your friend, and the self alone is your enemy.
meaning: You can be your own best friend or your own worst enemy. Growth starts when you decide to lift yourself.
explanation: Krishna uses one word, ātman, in two senses here: the higher self and the everyday self. Lift the everyday self up with the higher self; do not drag yourself down. You can be your own best friend (bandhu) or your own worst enemy (ripu). The following verse explains that the self is a friend to one who has mastered it, and an enemy to one who has not. It is an early, powerful call to self-responsibility: no one else can do your inner work for you.

story.title: From robber to poet
story.text: Tradition tells that Valmiki was once a highway robber named Ratnakara. When the sage Narada asked whether his family would share the burden of his sins, and they said no, he turned inward, meditated for years, and became the poet who wrote the Ramayana.

illustration.idea: A man in deep meditation as an anthill rises around him, the forest glowing softly.

teaching.title: Talk to yourself like a friend
teaching.practice: When you notice harsh self-talk today, rephrase it the way a good friend would say it to you.

test.question: Who can lift you up, according to this verse?
The self can be your...

sanskrit:
युक्ताहारविहारस्य युक्तचेष्टस्य कर्मसु।
युक्तस्वप्नावबोधस्य योगो भवति दुःखहा॥
transliteration:
yuktāhāra-vihārasya yukta-ceṣṭasya karmasu
yukta-svapnāvabodhasya yogo bhavati duḥkha-hā
translation: For one who is moderate in eating and recreation, balanced in work, and regular in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.
meaning: Spiritual life is built on simple, balanced daily habits. Not too much, not too little.
explanation: In chapter six Krishna teaches meditation, and he is practical. Yoga does not succeed for someone who overeats or starves, or who sleeps too much or too little. The word yukta means fitting or balanced. Balanced food (āhāra), balanced recreation (vihāra), balanced effort in work, and regular sleep and waking create the conditions where yoga becomes duḥkha-hā, the destroyer of sorrow. The spiritual path is built on simple daily habits.

story.title: Not too much, not too little
story.text: Just before this verse, Krishna warns that yoga is not for one who eats too much or starves, or who sleeps too much or too little. The path he teaches is one of balance, not extremes.

illustration.idea: A simple meal, a lamp and a bedroll arranged neatly in a sunlit hut, suggesting a balanced day.

teaching.title: One balanced habit
teaching.practice: Pick one area, food, screens or sleep, and bring it back to moderation today.

test.question: What does this verse recommend?
options: Moderation in food, work and sleep

test.question: For the balanced person, yoga becomes...

sanskrit:
यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम्।
ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत्॥
transliteration:
yato yato niścarati manaś cañcalam asthiram
tatas tato niyamyaitad ātmany eva vaśaṁ nayet
translation: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, from there one should draw it back and bring it under the control of the Self.
meaning: The mind will wander; that is its nature. The practice is simply to bring it back, again and again, without frustration.
explanation: Krishna knows the mind well. He calls it cañcala, restless, and asthira, unsteady. It will wander. The instruction is not to be harsh with it but to bring it back, every time, from wherever it has gone. A few verses later Arjuna admits the mind is as hard to hold as the wind, and Krishna agrees, adding that practice (abhyāsa) and letting go (vairāgya) make it possible. Every return is a small success.

story.title: The eye of the bird
story.text: In the Mahabharata, the teacher Drona placed a wooden bird in a tree and asked his students what they saw. Some saw the tree, the branches, their brothers. Arjuna said he saw only the bird's eye, and only he was allowed to shoot.

illustration.idea: A young archer drawing his bow, everything blurred except a small wooden bird's eye in sharp focus.

teaching.title: Bring it back
teaching.practice: Do one task today with full attention. Each time your mind wanders, gently bring it back without scolding yourself.

test.question: What should you do when the mind wanders?
In the story, what did Arjuna see?

sanskrit:
अनन्याश्चिन्तयन्तो मां ये जनाः पर्युपासते।
तेषां नित्याभियुक्तानां योगक्षेमं वहाम्यहम्॥
transliteration:
ananyāś cintayanto māṁ ye janāḥ paryupāsate
teṣāṁ nityābhiyuktānāṁ yoga-kṣemaṁ vahāmy aham
translation: To those who worship me with single-minded devotion, always united with me, I bring what they lack and preserve what they have.
meaning: Wholehearted trust brings a deep sense of being looked after. You are not carrying your life alone.
explanation: Chapter nine is called the royal secret. Here Krishna speaks to those who are ananya, whose devotion is not divided, who think of him and stay connected. To them he promises yoga-kṣema. Yoga here means gaining what you lack and kṣema means keeping what you have. In other words, he carries their welfare. This verse is beloved in India and is often seen on homes and offices as a reminder that sincere trust is answered.

keywords.meaning: gaining what is needed and keeping what is gained

story.title: Draupadi's call
story.text: When Draupadi was dragged into the royal court and humiliated, no elder came to her help. She raised her hands and called on Krishna with complete trust, and the cloth kept growing endlessly so she could not be shamed.

illustration.idea: A woman with hands raised in prayer as an endless stream of bright cloth flows around her in a royal hall.

teaching.title: Hand over one worry
teaching.practice: Write down one worry you cannot control. Offer it up in your own words, then turn your attention to what you can do.

test.question: What does Krishna promise single-minded devotees?
options: To bring what they lack and keep what they have

test.question: In the story, who called on Krishna for help?

sanskrit:
पत्रं पुष्पं फलं तोयं यो मे भक्त्या प्रयच्छति।
तदहं भक्त्युपहृतमश्नामि प्रयतात्मनः॥
transliteration:
patraṁ puṣpaṁ phalaṁ toyaṁ yo me bhaktyā prayacchati
tad ahaṁ bhakty-upahṛtam aśnāmi prayatātmanaḥ
translation: Whoever offers me with love a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, that offering of love from a pure heart I accept.
meaning: It is the love behind a gift that matters, not its size or cost.
explanation: After describing his vast cosmic forms, Krishna becomes tender. He asks for nothing grand: a leaf (patra), a flower (puṣpa), a fruit (phala) or water (toya). What matters is bhakti, love, and a sincere heart. This verse is the foundation of the simple offerings made in Indian homes every day. It also teaches a wider truth: the value of any gift lies in the love and attention behind it, not in its price.

keywords.meaning: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water

story.title: Sudama's rice
story.text: Sudama, Krishna's poor childhood friend, visited him in Dwaraka with only a handful of flattened rice wrapped in cloth. Embarrassed, he tried to hide it, but Krishna took it and ate it with joy, treasuring it above any royal gift.

illustration.idea: A king in fine robes joyfully eating rice from a worn cloth bundle, a thin poor man watching with tears.

teaching.title: Give small, give with love
teaching.practice: Offer something small today, a kind note, a cup of tea, a flower, with full attention and love.

test.question: What matters most in an offering, according to this verse?
What did Sudama bring to Krishna?

sanskrit:
अद्वेष्टा सर्वभूतानां मैत्रः करुण एव च।
निर्ममो निरहङ्कारः समदुःखसुखः क्षमी॥
transliteration:
adveṣṭā sarva-bhūtānāṁ maitraḥ karuṇa eva ca
nirmamo nirahaṅkāraḥ sama-duḥkha-sukhaḥ kṣamī
translation: One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and ego, even-minded in pain and pleasure, and forgiving, is dear to me.
meaning: This is a portrait of a good heart: no hatred, plenty of kindness, little ego, and an easy willingness to forgive.
explanation: Chapter twelve is about bhakti, and verses 13 to 20 describe the qualities of a person dear to God. This first verse lists several: free of hatred toward any being, friendly (maitra), compassionate (karuṇa), without possessiveness or ego, steady in pain and pleasure, and forgiving (kṣamī). Notice that these are not rituals but qualities of character. Many people read these verses slowly as a checklist for who they want to become.

story.title: Yudhishthira and the dog
story.text: At the end of the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira climbs toward heaven followed by a faithful dog. When told he may enter but the dog may not, he refuses to abandon it. The dog reveals itself as Dharma, his father, testing his compassion.

illustration.idea: A king standing at a radiant gate, refusing to step through, a small dog at his feet on a snowy mountain.

teaching.title: Forgive one thing
teaching.practice: Choose one small hurt you are holding on to and decide to let it go today.

test.question: Which quality is listed in this verse?
In the story, why did Yudhishthira refuse to enter heaven?
options: He would not abandon the dog

sanskrit:
सर्वधर्मान्परित्यज्य मामेकं शरणं व्रज।
अहं त्वां सर्वपापेभ्यो मोक्षयिष्यामि मा शुचः॥
transliteration:
sarva-dharmān parityajya mām ekaṁ śaraṇaṁ vraja
ahaṁ tvāṁ sarva-pāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ
translation: Setting aside all other duties, take refuge in me alone. I will free you from all wrongs. Do not grieve.
meaning: After all the teachings, the final word is trust. Let go of anxiety and rest in the divine.
explanation: This is often called the carama śloka, the final and crowning verse of the Gita's teaching. After eighteen chapters on action, knowledge, meditation and devotion, Krishna says: set aside every other support and take refuge (śaraṇa) in me alone. I will free you from all wrongs. Do not grieve. Teachers explain it in different ways, but all agree it is about complete trust. The Gita began with Arjuna's grief, and it ends with mā śucaḥ, do not grieve.

story.title: Arjuna's doubt is gone
story.text: After hearing this final teaching, Arjuna tells Krishna that his confusion is destroyed and his memory restored. He picks up his bow, ready to act. The conversation that began with grief ends with clarity.

illustration.idea: Arjuna standing tall in the chariot with his bow raised, Krishna holding the reins, light breaking over the battlefield.

teaching.title: Rest in trust
teaching.practice: Before sleeping tonight, let go of the day's worries one by one and say: I have done my part.

test.question: What does Krishna tell Arjuna not to do?
Where does this verse appear in the Gita?
options: Near the end, in the last chapter
It is not in the Gita
